concept.name: Inverted hammer
concept.definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal: buyers mounted an intraperiod rally that sellers could not fully erase, hinting that demand is emerging; confirmation by a higher close next period is normally required.
concept.intuition: In a falling market, buyers finally staged a real push upward during the session; even though it was sold back toward the open, the attempt shows bulls are waking up.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: the upper shadow (H - max(O, C)) is at least about twice the real body |C - O|, the lower shadow (min(O, C) - L) is very small, and the body sits near the low, after a preceding decline. The same shape after an uptrend is a shooting star.
concept.failure_modes: Because it closes near its low, the inverted hammer by itself still shows sellers winning the session, and downtrends often continue. Without bullish confirmation it is one of the weaker single-candle reversal candidates.
concept.misconceptions: It is not a shooting star: the two have identical geometry but opposite context and meaning. And it is not a buy signal on its own; the standard use requires the next candle to close higher.
concept.example: In a downtrend, a stock opens at 15.00, spikes to 16.20, and settles back to close at 15.05. A close above 15.50 the next session would be taken as confirmation that the inverted hammer marked a bottoming attempt.
